per_pair.why: B opens with a whoosh and dialogue blips that resolve into a composed, full-band track with beat, harmony and melody, while A loops one flat, buzzy pulse-wave arpeggio at a nearly constant level (0.3 LU range) with no melody or event to hook the player.

B's combat room has a continuous, layered track with melody and percussion across the whole spectrum, while A is a sparse kick-and-bass pulse over a quiet drone, with large empty gaps in the spectrogram and no melodic line, so it feels unfinished.

A's swing and hit sounds are short, sharp transients that stand about 16 dB above the music and read clearly, while B's attacks are long (0.3-0.5 s) broadband noise slabs that blank out the music and blur one hit into the next.

Close up, A's impacts have a crisp attack and a quick decay, with the pitched music still visible between and under them, while B's impacts are flat-topped white-noise blocks with no transient shape, so they sound like static rather than a hit.

loser_biggest_gap: The music is thin and uncomposed: it is a single repeating pulse-wave arpeggio on the title screen, and only a drum-and-bass pulse with no melody in combat. Write real tracks with a melodic lead, chord movement and a counter-line, plus layered pads or textures that fill the mid and upper range, so the title and the fight each have a theme that carries the moment.
loser_other_gaps: Give the title screen an arrival moment (a sting, whoosh or UI blip) and some dynamic shape, instead of an arpeggio that starts at full level and never changes (0.3 LU loudness range).
Fill the empty spectrum in the idle-combat state: add ambience or room tone and a sustained harmonic bed, so the silence between the kick hits does not sound like missing audio.
Soften the harsh, evenly spaced pulse-wave harmonics that reach about 15 kHz, using filtering, a variety of duty cycles or other timbres, so long listening is not fatiguing.
Vary the arrangement over time (sections, fills, instruments dropping in and out) so the loop does not read as one mechanical pattern.
reasoning: B sounds like a produced game soundtrack. Its opening has a clear arrival moment and its music is composed, with melody, harmony and percussion in every state. A's music is a bare procedural chip loop with no melody in the combat-idle state. A clearly wins on combat feedback: its hits are punchy, short and well above the music, while B's attack sounds are long broadband noise bursts that mask the score and smear together. Satisfying hit feedback matters a lot, but A's music is thin and monotonous across all four moments, and B's problem is narrower and fixable in the mix (shorter, shaped impact sounds). So B wins the overall soundscape by a slight margin.
